narrative:
The company’s system analyzed your work situation and concluded that there’s a **57% chance** you might leave your job soon. This isn’t a guess—it’s based on patterns from thousands of other employees in similar roles. When this probability reaches **40% or higher**, the system flags the case, and promotions are temporarily paused to prevent losing valuable talent. Unfortunately, your profile fell into this category, which is why your promotion was denied.

The decision wasn’t random—it was driven by three key factors. First, the system noticed that **you’ve been presented with other job opportunities** while working here. This is the strongest signal in your case, as it suggests you might be actively exploring alternatives. Unlike most employees (80% of whom haven’t received external offers), this experience made the system more cautious about your long-term commitment.

Second, your **length of time in this role** played a role, but in a surprising way. While you’ve been here for **6–10 years**—which is actually above average for employees who *do* get promoted—your tenure hasn’t been paired with the same level of recognition or growth opportunities as those who stay longer. Many employees with 11+ years in their jobs (only 15% of the promoted group) tend to feel more settled, but your situation suggests the company may need to reinforce your engagement to match that stability.

Finally, the system picked up on your **perception of fairness in promotions**. You’ve indicated that you *do* feel you’ve received the promotions you deserved so far, which is actually better than most employees (only 62% of promoted peers share this view). However, the system may be interpreting this as a sign that you expect *more* in the future—especially since your current role hasn’t included bonuses, overtime pay, or frequent business travel, all of which are common in higher-level positions.

Here’s what you can do next: **Ask for a one-on-one with your manager** to discuss your career path. Highlight your long-term experience (6–10 years in this company) and how you’ve contributed, while also expressing interest in addressing the gaps the system identified—like exploring internal growth opportunities or adjusting your compensation to reflect your value. Many employees in your position have successfully turned these conversations into promotions by showing they’re committed to staying while also advocating for their needs.
